stem: A fraud dataset has 0.2% positive cases. A classifier predicts every transaction as legitimate and obtains 99.8% accuracy. What is the strongest immediate criticism?

options.A: Accuracy is dominated by the majority class and can hide near-zero recall for fraud.
options.B: Accuracy is mathematically impossible on imbalanced data.
options.C: The model must have perfect calibration.

rationales.correct: With extreme class imbalance, the majority-class baseline can obtain high accuracy while completely failing the minority class. Precision, recall, PR-AUC, cost-sensitive metrics, and threshold analysis may be more informative.
rationales.B: Accuracy remains mathematically valid; it is the interpretation that is problematic.
rationales.C: Accuracy says nothing about probability calibration.
rationales.D: A constant-negative classifier has ROC-AUC around 0.5 under standard score conventions, not necessarily zero.

stem: For a rare-event detector, the business cost of false negatives is much higher than false positives. Which evaluation design is most appropriate?

options.A: Choose and report metrics and an operating threshold that explicitly reflect the asymmetric costs, such as recall at an acceptable precision or expected cost.
options.B: Optimize accuracy at a fixed threshold of 0.5 regardless of costs.
options.C: Ignore the confusion matrix because it is threshold-dependent.

rationales.correct: Classification metrics depend on the operating threshold, and threshold selection should reflect the actual cost of errors. A cost matrix can be converted into expected cost or used to select a point on the precision-recall tradeoff.
rationales.B: A 0.5 threshold has no universal decision-theoretic justification.
rationales.C: Threshold dependence is a reason to analyze the confusion matrix, not ignore it.
rationales.D: Training loss does not measure the business operating point.

stem: Why is fitting a StandardScaler on the entire dataset before cross-validation a form of leakage?

options.A: The scaling parameters (mean and variance) use information from validation folds, allowing held-out data to influence training transformations.
options.C: StandardScaler can only be used after cross-validation is complete.

rationales.correct: Any learned preprocessing parameter must be estimated using the training portion of each fold. Otherwise the held-out fold contributes information to the feature transformation.
rationales.C: The scaler should be inside a pipeline so each fold fits it on its training split.
rationales.D: Scaled features are perfectly compatible with cross-validation when preprocessing is correctly nested.

stem: You have multiple records per patient and want to estimate performance on unseen patients. Which split strategy is most defensible?

options.A: Group-aware splitting so records from the same patient do not appear in both training and evaluation folds.
options.B: Randomly split individual rows without considering patient identity.
options.C: Put all patients in every fold and average the training scores.
options.D: Duplicate each patient into every fold to increase sample size.

rationales.correct: Patient-level dependence makes row-wise random splitting optimistic because the model can exploit patient-specific signals seen in training. Group-aware cross-validation keeps groups disjoint.
rationales.B: This risks leakage through repeated subjects.
rationales.C: Training scores are not an out-of-sample estimate.
rationales.D: Duplicating groups across folds violates independence.

stem: What is the fundamental purpose of a final untouched test set after model selection?

options.A: To provide a final estimate of generalization after the model, preprocessing choices, and hyperparameters have been selected without using that test set.
options.C: To tune the learning rate until performance peaks.
options.D: To increase the effective training sample count by copying labels.

rationales.correct: A final holdout protects the estimate from selection bias caused by repeated experimentation. It should be used sparingly, ideally only for final assessment.
rationales.B: The test set is not part of gradient computation.
rationales.C: Using the test set for tuning defeats its role.
rationales.D: Test data should not be duplicated into training just to increase sample count.

stem: Which statement about stratified cross-validation in classification is most accurate?

options.A: It attempts to preserve class proportions across folds, which can make estimates more stable when class frequencies matter.
options.B: It guarantees every fold has identical predictions.
options.C: It eliminates all forms of data leakage automatically.
options.D: It is equivalent to training one model on the full dataset.

rationales.correct: Stratification preserves approximate class composition across folds. It addresses split representation, not every other experimental-design problem.
rationales.B: It controls sampling proportions, not predictions.
rationales.C: Preprocessing leakage and grouping issues still require appropriate pipelines/splitters.

stem: A model's ROC-AUC is high, but its precision is unacceptable at the production threshold. What is the correct conclusion?

options.A: Ranking quality may be good, but the chosen operating threshold or probability quality is not meeting the deployment requirement.
options.B: The ROC-AUC calculation must be wrong.
options.C: High ROC-AUC mathematically guarantees high precision at every threshold.

rationales.correct: ROC-AUC summarizes ranking across thresholds and is not a guarantee about any single operating point. Precision is also prevalence-sensitive.
rationales.B: The two metrics answer different questions and can legitimately disagree at a threshold.
rationales.C: AUC does not guarantee threshold-specific precision.
rationales.D: Precision = TP/(TP+FP) depends strongly on base rates for a fixed detector quality.

stem: A probability model predicts 0.8 on a group of examples, and about 80% of those examples are actually positive. What property does this suggest?

options.A: Calibration at that probability level: among cases predicted near 0.8, the empirical positive frequency is near 0.8.
options.C: The classifier has 80% recall regardless of threshold.
options.D: The model ranks every positive above every negative.

rationales.correct: Calibration concerns agreement between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies. One well-calibrated probability bin does not establish global calibration.
rationales.C: Recall is a separate thresholded metric.
rationales.D: Ranking quality is not implied by calibration.
